title: Scenario 3 — Utilities & Roadworks
subtitle: 400 m of new water main along a suburban high street: open-cut trenching, buried services, live traffic, confined space chamber work and highway reinstatement.

brief.client: Midshire Water (utility company, working under street works permits from the highway authority)
brief.location: Suburban high street with shops, residential side roads, a school crossing and a public car park used for the site compound
description: You are the Site Manager for 400 m of new 315 mm water main laid by open-cut trenching to 2.1 m deep along a busy suburban high street, plus connections into a deep existing chamber.

The works involve trench boxes, congested buried services (gas, HV electricity, telecoms), temporary traffic management with a lane closure and portable signals, pedestrian diversions past occupied shops, spoil handling, dewatering and reinstatement to highway standards.
A section near the school crossing must be completed at night to an agreed window, and every metre of highway you occupy is controlled by street works permits and notices.
You must plan the street works, set up a safe linear site, control the high-risk activities and hand the highway back in a condition the authority will accept.
constraints: Live traffic in the remaining lane throughout, controlled by portable signals
Shops must keep pedestrian access and deliveries during trading hours
School crossing within the works length — night working agreed for that section
Street works permit conditions set the dates, hours and length of highway you may occupy
Compound limited to one corner of the public car park
Known congested services: low and medium pressure gas, HV cable crossing, telecoms ducts
keyRisks: Striking buried services — gas mains and an HV cable crossing
Trench collapse at 2.1 m and entry into unsupported excavation
Traffic incursion into the works and plant/pedestrian conflict
Confined space entry for the deep chamber connection
Lifting and lowering pipes with the excavator near people in and around the trench
Spoil surcharge at the trench edge, flooding and dewatering discharge
Public interface — shoppers, residents, children near the school crossing

cppProjectDescription: Installation of 400 m of new 315 mm water main by open-cut trenching to 2.1 m along a suburban high street, including trench box support, connections into a deep existing chamber (confined space), temporary traffic management with lane closure and portable signals, pedestrian diversions past shops, dewatering, spoil management and reinstatement to highway standards. Duration 16 weeks; night working for the section at the school crossing. Works carried out under street works permits and noticing to the highway authority.

phases.title: Project Brief
phases.intro: Understand what you are taking on before a single cone goes out. Street works add a second rulebook: the highway authority controls when and where you may work.

steps.title: Your project
body: You are the Site Manager for a 16-week, £1.1m water main renewal along a trading high street. The road stays live, the shops stay open, and the school stays in session.

Unlike a fenced construction site, your workplace is a moving strip of highway. The public are an arm's length away for the whole job, and the ground below you is congested with gas, electricity and telecoms.
Every decision you make will affect safety, legal compliance, programme, cost, quality, the environment, client confidence, workforce morale, enforcement risk and the likelihood of an accident.
keyPoints: Street works permits and notices control your occupation of the highway — dates, hours and length
The killers on this job are service strikes, trench collapse and live traffic — plan for those first
Keeping traffic and shoppers moving never justifies working in an unsupported trench or digging blind

steps.prompt: The programme shows you occupying the highway from Monday, but the street works permit for the first section has not yet been granted. The contracts manager says 'get the cones out — the permit will catch up'. What do you do?
steps.context: The compound corner of the car park has been licensed to you separately and is available now.

options.text: Hold off the highway until the permit is granted and its conditions are read. Meanwhile mobilise the licensed compound, finish the service record review and TM checks, and press the authority for a decision.
options.feedback: Correct. Occupying the highway without a granted permit is an offence and the fastest way to lose the authority's trust. The off-highway preparation you can lawfully do is exactly how you protect the programme.

options.text: Keep the TM crew and plant booked for Monday so the slot isn't lost, ask the authority's coordinator for an early decision, and stand everyone down on Sunday evening if the permit still hasn't been confirmed by then.
options.feedback: Holding resources against a permit that may not land burns money, and a Sunday-night stand-down rarely happens — the pressure to start anyway is how unlawful starts occur. Confirm the permit first, then commit resources.

options.text: Set out the advance signs and the taper on Monday so drivers settle into the new layout ahead of the dig, but keep the excavator off the carriageway until the permit is confirmed — no ground gets broken without it.
options.feedback: Signing and coning is occupation of the highway. The permit governs the whole street works activity, not just the excavation.
options.consequence: The authority's inspector found signs and a taper out with no granted permit and recorded unpermitted occupation; a fixed penalty followed and the first section's permit was delayed further.

options.text: Start trenching Monday as programmed — the application went in on time, the delay is the authority's own, and starting now protects the night window agreed with the school for the crossing section.
options.feedback: Unlawful occupation, no agreed TM conditions, and a coordination system deliberately bypassed — a submitted application is not a permit. Authorities issue fixed penalties, stop works and remember who did this at every future permit application.
options.criticalFailure: Occupied the highway and broke ground without a street works permit
options.consequence: A street works inspector found the trench open with no permit or agreed TM; the authority issued a fixed penalty and stopped the works, and the client's later applications drew closer scrutiny.

steps.topic: NRSWA — street works permits and noticing
steps.learningNote: Street works legislation requires works on the highway to be noticed or permitted before they start, with conditions covering dates, hours, TM and length of occupation. Coordinating with the highway authority is a planning activity, not paperwork after the event.

phases.title: Pre-Construction Planning
phases.intro: Establish who holds which duties and confirm the people doing the work are competent for street works, excavations and confined spaces.

steps.prompt: Midshire Water asks you to confirm the CDM 2015 duty holder arrangements for the project. Which is correct?
steps.context: There is a groundworks contractor, a traffic management contractor and a reinstatement contractor, a design team, and around 18 people at peak over 16 weeks.

options.text: Midshire Water is the client and appoints a principal designer and principal contractor in writing; the job is notifiable, so an F10 goes in; the highway authority is a key stakeholder, not a CDM duty holder.
options.feedback: Correct. More than one contractor means the client must appoint a PD and PC in writing. Over 30 working days with 20+ workers simultaneously, or 500 person-days, triggers F10 notification — a 16-week utilities project usually exceeds 500 person-days. The authority controls the highway, but it holds no CDM duty.

options.text: Street works on the highway run under their own statutory regime — permits, qualified supervisors, authority inspections and reinstatement standards — so those arrangements stand in for CDM duty holder appointments on this job.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Street works legislation and CDM apply in parallel. Laying a main is construction work; the permit regime adds duties, it doesn't replace them.
options.consequence: The client's audit found no PD or PC appointed and no F10; work paused while appointments, notification and the CPP were put in place, and the client questioned the planning.

options.text: The highway authority is the client in practice: it owns the road, sets the permit conditions, inspects the works and signs off the reinstatement, so it should be the one appointing the principal contractor and principal designer.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The client is the organisation for whom the project is carried out — the water company. The authority grants permission to occupy its asset.
options.consequence: The authority declined to act as client, leaving nobody formally appointed; the client's audit stopped mobilisation while the appointments and F10 were completed, costing several days.

options.text: The framework agreement already sets out who normally does what on Midshire Water jobs, so project appointments add nothing and the gangs can mobilise under those standing roles.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Standing framework roles are not project appointments. Without explicit written appointments, nobody legally plans, manages and coordinates a construction phase full of fatal risks — and framework assumptions collapse the first time two contractors clash in the trench.
options.criticalFailure: No formal CDM duty holder appointments on a multi-contractor project
options.consequence: With no appointed PC, nobody coordinated a TM lane switch with the trench gang and a van entered the works. HSE investigated, found no appointments or F10, and served an improvement notice.

steps.topic: CDM 2015 — duty holders on utility projects
steps.learningNote: CDM 2015 applies to street works exactly as it does to a building site. The utility client appoints the principal designer and principal contractor in writing; F10 notification depends on duration and person-days, not on the type of work.

cppText.best: Client: Midshire Water. Principal Designer and Principal Contractor appointed in writing; F10 notified to HSE and displayed at the compound. Groundworks, TM and reinstatement contractors briefed on their CDM duties. Highway authority engaged as permit-granting stakeholder with named coordination contact.
cppText.partial: Duty holders identified but written appointment evidence incomplete.
cppText.poor: Duty holder allocation unclear — assumed to sit under street works arrangements.
cppText.unsafe: No formal CDM appointments before works commenced — non-compliant.

steps.prompt: How do you satisfy yourself that the workforce is competent for this project?
steps.context: The work needs streetworks-qualified operatives and supervisors, trained TM installers, excavator operators, and a small team for the confined space chamber connection.

options.text: Verify before start: street works qualifications for operatives and supervisors, TM training for the guarding crew, plant cards, confined space and rescue training for the chamber team, and each contractor's RAMS quality.
options.feedback: Correct. Street works law requires qualified operatives and supervisors on the works; confined space entry and rescue need specific training; and RAMS quality shows whether the organisation behind the cards is capable.

options.text: Require a current CSCS card for every operative and SSSTS for every supervisor, collect the cards at induction, and have each contractor confirm in writing that their people are trained for the specific tasks they've been given.
options.feedback: General cards and a written assurance prove basic awareness, not street works qualification, confined space competence or plant tickets. Competence checks must match the risk of the task — and be verified, not promised.

options.text: Rely on the competence clause in each subcontract and the contractors' prequalification audits — they've already vetted their people, and repeating the checks only duplicates effort.
options.feedback: You cannot contract out the duty to take reasonable steps. A clause is a promise and a company prequalification says nothing about the individuals who turn up; competence checking is verification.
options.consequence: A sample inspection by the authority found an operative digging near the gas main with no street works qualification; the gang was stood down for a day and a defect was recorded.

options.text: Let the gangs start and have the supervisors watch the first few shifts closely, moving anyone who isn't up to it off the tools — on a job like this, how someone handles a breaker beside a gas main is a truer test than a wallet full of cards.
options.feedback: Unsafe. By the time incompetence 'looks unsure' next to a gas main or inside a chamber, the exposure has already happened.
options.criticalFailure: Workforce deployed on high-risk utility work without competence verification
options.consequence: An operative with no confined space training climbed into the chamber to free a valve and collapsed; the fire service recovered him to hospital and HSE served a prohibition notice.

steps.topic: Competence — street works, plant and confined spaces
steps.learningNote: Match the check to the risk: street works qualifications for those executing and supervising works in the highway, specific training for TM installation, plant categories for the machines on site, and confined space entry and rescue training before anyone plans to enter the chamber.

cppText.best: Competence verified before start: streetworks-qualified operatives and supervisors on all highway works; TM crew trained for signing, lighting and guarding; plant operator cards checked; chamber team trained in confined space entry, gas detection and rescue; RAMS quality reviewed as part of contractor assessment. Records held at the compound; induction mandatory.
cppText.partial: Core cards checked; confined space and TM training evidence to be completed before those activities.
cppText.poor: Competence assumed from contract clauses — verification not done.
cppText.unsafe: No competence verification for high-risk activities.

steps.prompt: Put the pre-construction activities for the water main in a safe, lawful order — from appointments through to the first break of ground in the high street.
steps.context: Midshire Water wants a start on the first section as soon as possible. The route crosses medium-pressure gas, an HV cable and telecoms ducts, and every metre of highway you occupy needs a granted permit.

activities.label: Client appoints PD and PC in writing; F10 submitted
activities.detail: Midshire Water confirms the duty holders so pre-construction information and planning have owners.

activities.label: Gather utility records and commission a PAS 128 survey
activities.detail: Undertakers' plans collected, then detection and verification of services along the 400 m route.

activities.label: Fix trench alignment and TM design around the services
activities.detail: Route, working width, lane closure, signals and pedestrian diversion designed from the survey results.

activities.label: Submit street works permit applications
activities.detail: Applications to the highway authority with the TM layout, dates, hours and extent for each section.

activities.label: Prepare CPP, review RAMS and open the TW register
activities.detail: Plan covers the initial works and strike and collapse emergencies; TWC appointed; box data checked.

activities.label: Permit granted; notify residents, shops and the school
activities.detail: Conditions read and briefed; letter-drop and school liaison before any occupation of the highway.

activities.label: Mobilise compound, induct gang, install TM to layout
activities.detail: Compound in the car park corner; inductions and card checks; TM set out in the approved sequence.

activities.label: Permit to dig, CAT & Genny and trial holes; first dig
activities.detail: Services located and marked on the ground, positions proven by hand-dug trial holes before the machine digs.

constraints.reason: The principal contractor draws up the construction phase plan — it has no author until the PC is appointed.
The trench line, working width and therefore the TM layout depend on where the services actually are.
Permit applications must carry the proposed TM, extent and dates — the authority assesses the application against them.
A permit is only granted on an application; applying late compresses the authority's notice periods and your start.
Placing cones and signs is occupying the highway — it needs a granted permit, and frontagers must be told first.
The construction phase, compound set-up included, must not start until a suitable CPP is in place.
Breaking ground without records and a survey of the gas, HV and telecoms is digging blind beside live services.
Nobody excavates in the carriageway until the agreed TM is in place to protect the gang from live traffic.

steps.topic: Pre-construction sequencing — CDM 2015, PAS 128 and street works permits
steps.learningNote: Information before design, design before application, permit before occupation, plan before construction, protection before excavation. Utility records and a PAS 128 survey shape the trench line and the TM; the TM design goes in with the permit application; nothing is placed in the highway until the permit is granted and the CPP is in place; and the first dig waits for the TM, a permit to dig and trial holes.

phases.title: Construction Phase Plan
phases.intro: Your CPP must reflect a moving linear site: the hazards travel along the street with you, and the arrangements must work at every chainage.

steps.prompt: The CPP is drafted, but the service strike emergency plan and the TM drawings for the first section are unfinished. Midshire Water wants the start date held. Can the construction phase begin?

options.text: No. Before anyone works in the highway the plan must cover the initial works — welfare, the service strike and trench emergency arrangements, and the agreed TM layout. Finish those, then start.
options.feedback: Correct. On this job the emergency arrangements and TM are not appendices — they are the controls for the first hour of work. A short, explained delay protects the client from something far worse.

options.text: Start the compound set-up and off-highway preparation on the planned date and finish the outstanding CPP sections in parallel, so the plan is complete before the first excavation in the highway.
options.feedback: Workable only if the plan genuinely covers what is being done — but welfare and emergency arrangements are needed from the first day of any construction work, including compound set-up.

options.text: Start on time with the trench gang using the draft CPP and the groundworker's RAMS, which already cover the main hazards, and get the strike plan and TM drawings signed off by the end of week one.
options.feedback: The construction phase must not start until a suitable plan is in place. Week one on this project includes trenching next to gas — the highest-risk period, not a warm-up.
options.consequence: On the first morning the gang exposed an unrecorded gas service; with no strike plan nobody knew the emergency number or cordon distance, and the job stood for half a day.

options.text: Issue the company's standard streetworks CPP — it already covers excavation, TM and service strikes — and start Monday, adding the site-specific detail as each new section of the run is opened up.
options.feedback: A template that doesn't name this street's gas main, HV crossing, school or TM layout controls nothing. Paper compliance with real hazards is how service strikes happen.
options.criticalFailure: Construction phase started under a generic plan with no site-specific emergency or TM arrangements
options.consequence: The generic plan never identified the MP gas main; the excavator gouged it and caused an escape. The parade was evacuated, a dangerous occurrence was reported and HSE served a notice.

steps.topic: CDM 2015 — construction phase plan for street works
steps.learningNote: The CPP must be in place before the construction phase begins and must be proportionate and site-specific. For street works that means the service records, the TM arrangements and the emergency plan for strikes and collapse are in the plan before the first cut, and the plan moves with the works.

cppText.best: Site rules issued before start: induction mandatory; permit to dig before any break of ground; no entry to any unsupported excavation; no one in the trench during lifting or box handling; high-visibility clothing to the standard required for highway works at all times; TM not altered except by trained TM operatives; plant keys controlled; no work outside permitted hours or length.
cppText.partial: Interim site rules issued; full set completed in week one.
cppText.poor: Site rules incomplete at start of works.
cppText.unsafe: No site rules in place — generic plan issued unedited.

phases.title: Site Set-Up
phases.intro: Lay out the street works site. The shops and footway are at the top, the coned working lane holds the trench run, live traffic passes in the remaining lane, and your compound sits in the car park corner. Think segregation: shoppers, traffic, plant and the open trench.

steps.prompt: Place the site set-up items. Shop frontages and the footway run along the top; the trench run and chamber sit in the coned working lane; live traffic uses the far lane past the school crossing; the compound occupies the car park corner. Place every required item where it is safest and most practical.

rules.placementNote: Continuous fencing/barrier between the works and the public — around the compound and along the working lane. Fencing dumped on the footway blocks the pedestrian diversion.
Controlled vehicle access into the compound from the car park side, never through the footway or the crossing.
Advance warning and information signing on the approaches and at the diversion — signs standing in the excavation protect nobody.
Lighting to the works, barriers and pedestrian diversion — essential for the night working section and dark winter afternoons.
Compound security — plant, fuel and materials in a public car park attract attention overnight.
Barriered, ramped pedestrian diversion along the footway past the shops — never share the working lane with plant or route people beside the open trench.
Plant and delivery movements stay within the coned working lane and compound, marshalled at pinch points.
Signing, lighting and guarding to the agreed layout: taper, safety zone, portable signals, and specific protection at the school crossing.
Welfare in the compound, a short walk from the works — not in the live working lane.
Toilets and washing with the welfare cabin — shop facilities are not compliant provision.
Site office and induction point in the compound, where the permits and service drawings live.
First aid point at the compound, signed, with arrangements to reach an injured person anywhere along the 400 m.
Fire point at the compound near the fuel store and generators.
Muster in the compound, upwind options briefed in case of a gas escape on the main run.
Spill kits at the refuelling point and with the pump/dewatering set-up — spills happen where the plant is, not where the store is.
Skips in the compound or laydown, clear of the footway and the gully.
Pipes stored in the laydown area, chocked against rolling — never stacked on the footway or over the gully.
Bunded fuel storage in the secure compound, as far as the site allows from the roadside gully.
Plant parked overnight in the compound or laydown with keys removed — never left in the working lane or near the crossing.
The excavation stays inside the guarded working lane — the trench run and the chamber dig.
Exclusion zone around the excavator's slew radius and the chamber entry — nobody inside it during lifting or box handling.
Protect the roadside gully from silt, spills and dewatering discharge — it drains to a watercourse, not a treatment works.
Continuous pedestrian barriers, trench covers/footbridges at crossing points, and dedicated protection where the school crossing meets the works.
Noise screening/monitoring for the night working section near homes and the school.

steps.topic: Street works site set-up and segregation
steps.learningNote: A linear street works site is a set of moving corridors: pedestrians on a protected diverted footway, traffic behind the taper and safety zone, plant and the trench inside the guarded working lane, and everything static — welfare, fuel, pipes, parking — off the highway in the compound. Fuel and silt stay away from the gully; barriers stay continuous.

steps.prompt: How do you set up and run the temporary traffic management for the lane closure?

options.text: Trained TM operatives install the agreed layout in the approved sequence; the safety zone stays clear of people and materials; the signals run as agreed; and drive-through and walk-through checks are recorded at set times and after interference.
options.feedback: Correct. TM is engineering control for the highest-energy hazard on site — live traffic. The layout, the setting-out sequence, the safety zone discipline and the routine checks are all part of the control, not optional extras.

options.text: Let the experienced TM crew set the cones and signs each morning to suit where the trench head is, within the agreed lane closure — tapers and sign spacing change as the dig moves, so a fixed drawing goes stale within days.
options.feedback: Improvised layouts drift: tapers too short, signs missing, no safety zone. A moving site needs a TM design that covers each stage of the move — setting out is itself a high-risk task with a defined sequence, not a fresh improvisation every morning.
options.consequence: A taper set short one morning gave drivers little warning of the closure; a car clipped the cones and stopped in the safety zone. Nobody was hurt, but the authority's inspection failed the layout.

options.text: Use the safety zone as the strip for pipe stacks and the welfare van — it's already inside the cones, it keeps materials off the footway and it saves the shops losing their frontage.
options.feedback: The safety zone exists to absorb the errant vehicle. Putting people or materials in it converts your protection margin into a target.
options.criticalFailure: Safety zone occupied by people and materials
options.consequence: A van that misjudged the taper struck the pipe stack in the safety zone and shunted it into the working area; an operative suffered a broken leg and the incident was RIDDOR-reported.

options.text: Install the full agreed layout with trained operatives, then rely on the gang and the signals contractor to report knocked cones and blown signs during the shift, rather than tying a TM operative up on scheduled drive-through and walk-through checks.
options.feedback: Layouts degrade: cones get clipped, signs blow over, residents move barriers. Without drive-through and walk-through checks you won't know until something finds the gap.

steps.topic: Temporary traffic management — signing, lighting and guarding
steps.learningNote: Treat TM like temporary works: an agreed design, trained people installing in a safe sequence (signs first, from the far side of the works, protected), a safety zone that is never occupied, and recorded checks after setting out, during the shift and after weather, darkness or interference.

cppText.best: TM installed to the agreed signing, lighting and guarding layout by trained operatives; taper and safety zone maintained and never used for work or storage; portable signals operated to the permit conditions with manual control available at peak times; pedestrian diversion barriered, lit and ramped past shops; drive-through/walk-through checks at start, mid and end of shift and after weather or interference, recorded; school crossing given dedicated protection and timing arrangements.
cppText.partial: TM layout installed as designed; routine checking regime to be formalised.
cppText.poor: TM improvised daily by the gang without reference to the agreed layout.
cppText.unsafe: Safety zone compromised — used for people/materials.

phases.title: Welfare and Access
phases.intro: A linear site still owes its people proper welfare, and it owes the emergency services a way in. Plan both before the first shift.

steps.prompt: The gang will be working up to 400 m from the compound as the trench progresses. What welfare provision do you make?

options.text: Full welfare at the compound from day one — toilets, warm-water washing, drinking water, a heated rest and drying room — sized for the peak, with breaks and a shuttle planned so it's usable from every chainage.
options.feedback: Correct. Welfare must be provided from the first day and must be realistically accessible. On a linear site that means planning the distance, not just parking a cabin.

options.text: Agree a paid arrangement with two cafés along the route for toilets, handwashing and hot drinks — they're open all day, closer than any cabin, and the gang will actually use them.
options.feedback: Facilities you don't control are not compliant provision — they close, they refuse muddy boots, and they offer no proper washing, drying or rest space for a working gang.
options.consequence: One café closed for refurbishment and the other refused muddy boots; operatives began relieving themselves behind the spoil heap, a shopkeeper complained to the client and morale dropped.

options.text: Tow a self-contained toilet and handwash unit behind the works face so facilities are always within 50 m of the gang — on a linear site, distance matters more than a big heated cabin parked in the car park at one end.
options.feedback: A toilet and handwash trailer is not welfare: warm-water washing, drinking water, rest and drying facilities are all required — mobile works don't dilute the standard.
options.consequence: With no warm water, drying room or rest area, the gang ate in their vans in wet gear; two operatives developed dermatitis and the client's audit raised a welfare non-conformance.

options.text: Hold the start until a second full welfare unit can be hired and sited at the far end of the run, so nobody is ever more than 200 m from toilets, washing, drinking water and a heated rest room, whatever that does to the programme.
options.feedback: Compliant but heavy-handed — one well-placed compound with planned breaks and transport meets the duty on a 400 m run. Know what 'suitable and sufficient' looks like before you spend the programme.

steps.topic: Welfare on linear / mobile sites
steps.learningNote: Welfare duties apply in full to street works: toilets, washing with warm water, drinking water, rest and drying facilities from day one. On linear sites the test is real accessibility — plan break patterns, distances and transport so the provision is actually used.

cppText.best: Welfare at the compound from day one: toilets, washing with warm water, drinking water, heated rest room with means to warm food, drying room. Sized for peak workforce of 18. Break patterns and shuttle arrangements ensure access from all chainages, including the night shift. Cleaned and maintained daily.
cppText.partial: Compound welfare in place; access arrangements from far chainages to be confirmed.
cppText.poor: Welfare relies on informal arrangements with local premises.
cppText.unsafe: No compliant welfare at start of works.

steps.prompt: Set the emergency arrangements for this project before work starts.

options.text: A site plan for gas and HV strikes (numbers, evacuation distance, no re-entry), trench collapse (no hand-digging a casualty out unsupported), chamber rescue, first aid on every shift, ambulance access through the TM and chainage markers for 999 calls.
options.feedback: Correct. The foreseeable emergencies here — strike, collapse, confined space, traffic incursion — each need a rehearsed response, and the ambulance needs a way through your own signals.

options.text: First aiders on every day shift, a kit in each van and the 999 route briefed at induction — the hospital is ten minutes away and the fire service carries its own rescue equipment.
options.feedback: 999 does not dig a casualty out of a collapse, isolate an HV cable or ventilate a chamber. Emergency arrangements are what happens in the minutes before help arrives — and your TM can delay that help if you haven't planned access.

options.text: Adopt the groundworks contractor's emergency procedure, which already covers service strikes and excavation collapse, adding the site address and the gas and electricity emergency numbers.
options.feedback: Adding phone numbers to a generic procedure still leaves out the school contact, the signal head locations, ambulance access through the TM, chainage referencing and the chamber rescue kit. Site-specific or it isn't a plan.
options.consequence: When an operative collapsed at the far end of the run, the 999 call gave only the street name; the ambulance was held at the signals, and the delay drew a complaint and an internal review.

options.text: Write the strike, collapse and first aid arrangements now, then draft the chamber rescue plan once the connection design is fixed, since the rescue method depends on the access chosen.
options.feedback: Rescue equipment and trained people take time to procure and rehearse, and the rescue method should shape the access design, not follow it. Plans written the night before an entry are the ones that fail during one.
options.criticalFailure: Confined space work planned without rescue arrangements in place
options.consequence: The chamber rescue plan was still a draft when entry went ahead; an operative became unwell at the bottom with no retrieval rig set. The fire service recovered him and HSE served a prohibition notice.

steps.topic: Emergency planning — strikes, collapse and rescue
steps.learningNote: Plan for the emergencies this site can produce: gas strike (evacuate, no ignition sources, gas emergency number, cordon), HV strike (stay clear, treat as live, DNO), trench collapse (never dig by hand over a casualty without support in place), chamber rescue (equipment and trained people at the entry), and emergency service access through your own traffic management.

cppText.best: Emergency plan covers gas and HV service strikes with utility emergency numbers and evacuation distances, trench collapse response, confined space rescue at the chamber (tripod, harness, gas monitor, trained top man — no reliance on 999 for retrieval), first aid on every shift including nights, emergency access route through the TM agreed with the signals settings, and chainage/location referencing displayed for 999 calls. Muster at the compound with an upwind alternative briefed.
cppText.partial: Basic emergency plan in place; chamber rescue and emergency access arrangements to be completed before those phases.
cppText.poor: Generic emergency procedure adopted without site-specific detail.
cppText.unsafe: High-risk activities planned with no rescue arrangements.

phases.title: Hazard Identification
phases.intro: Walk the 400 m on paper. Which hazards get your management attention first, and where can fire and gas hurt people you can't see?

steps.prompt: Walk the live trench run before the school traffic builds. Flag every observation that needs action before work carries on — and leave alone the ones that are under control.
steps.location: Site walk-round — shop parade and school crossing section, 07:40 on a dry weekday morning

observations.text: Operative bedding pipe inside the trench box; ladder inside the box, its top about 1 m above ground level.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. He is working within the supported length, and the ladder sits inside the box and extends above the edge for a secure handhold — the access and entry standard the RAMS sets.

observations.text: Spoil heap about 1.5 m high with its toe at the trench lip, on the side where the boxes are set.
observations.explanation: Hazard. Spoil at the edge surcharges the ground and the box beyond the loading its tabulated data was checked for, and can slide in. Stop, pull it back to the registered stand-off and re-inspect the support before re-entry.

observations.text: Chain sling choked round a pipe and hooked over the bucket teeth; an operative waits in the trench to guide it.
observations.explanation: Hazard. Bucket teeth are not a lifting point and a person below a suspended load has nowhere to go. Stop the lift: rated lifting point or attachment, certified accessories, tag lines from outside the trench and nobody below.

observations.text: Road plate at the shop delivery entrance: bedded, pinned, ramped edges, permit to load signed this morning.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. A plate within its rated span, bedded and secured to the standard detail and released to traffic by a permit to load is the temporary works control working as intended.

observations.text: Excavator refuelling from the bowser over a drip tray, spill kit open alongside, nearby gully covered by a mat.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. Drip tray under the transfer, spill kit to hand and the drainage pathway sealed — this is the refuelling arrangement the environmental plan asks for.

observations.text: Two pedestrian barriers by the school crossing meet at an angle, leaving a gap of about 300 mm at the joint.
observations.explanation: Hazard. A child fits through 300 mm and the open 2.1 m trench is beyond it. Link the barriers into a continuous line now and check every joint before school arrival and pick-up times.

observations.text: Pressure test running: end caps braced against cast thrust blocks, bay taped off, gang working 40 m away.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. Designed thrust restraint plus an exclusion zone while pressure is on is the control for testing — nobody works near restrained ends until the main is depressurised.

observations.text: Operative in the trench trimming the face about a metre beyond the end of the last trench box.
observations.explanation: Hazard. That metre of face is unsupported ground at 2.1 m. Get him out: nobody works ahead of installed support — trim from above with the machine and advance the box.

observations.text: Four-gas monitor packed in the chamber entry kit; its bump-test log was last signed three days ago.
observations.explanation: Hazard. An unchecked monitor may not alarm, and the chamber entry depends on it. Bump-test before each day's use, record it, and quarantine any unit that fails or is out of calibration.

observations.text: Spoil heaped behind the barrier line at the stand-off marked on the RAMS sketch, no higher than the barriers.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. Spoil kept beyond the registered stand-off keeps surcharge off the trench and boxes, and a low heap won't spill into the excavation or onto the footway.

observations.text: Pedestrian barriers along the footway diversion clipped together at every joint, with a tapping rail at the base.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. A continuous, linked barrier with a tapping rail guides all pedestrians, including people with visual impairments, and keeps them clear of the works.

observations.text: Road plate over the side-road trench rocks and clanks each time a car crosses; no pins visible at the corners.
observations.explanation: Hazard. A rocking plate is unbedded or unsecured and can creep or tip under load over an open trench. Close it to traffic, re-bed and pin it to the standard detail, then reissue the permit to load before reopening.

observations.text: Excavator lowering a pipe from a rated lifting eye, bucket off, tag lines held by two operatives outside the trench.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. A rated lifting point, certified accessories and tag lines controlled from outside the trench with nobody below the load — the planned excavator lift in action.

observations.text: Fusion generator being topped up from a jerry can on the carriageway, a metre from an open gully.
observations.explanation: Hazard. Any spill runs straight to the drain, and decanting fuel beside the works adds an ignition risk near gas plant. Refuel at the planned position on a drip tray with a spill kit and the gully covered.

observations.text: Pump discharge hose laid flat across the diverted footway at the shop doorways, with no ramp or cover over it.
observations.explanation: Hazard. A trip for shoppers and an obstacle for pushchairs and wheelchair users on the diversion. Route it under a proprietary hose ramp or around the footway, and keep the pedestrian route clear.

observations.text: Banksman wearing a personal gas monitor; the card clipped to it shows today's bump test logged at 07:15.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. A personal monitor bump-tested and recorded before the shift is ready to warn of gas in the trench — exactly what the gas proximity controls require.

steps.topic: Hazard identification — street works site walk-round
steps.learningNote: On a linear street works site the same subjects recur along the whole run: spoil, boxes, plates, barriers, lifts, fuel and gas monitors. Know what 'right' looks like for each so the wrong version stands out — spoil at the stand-off, nobody beyond the support, plates bedded and released by permit to load, barriers linked at every joint, lifts on rated points with nobody below, fuel kept off the drains, and monitors bump-tested on the day.

steps.prompt: Which set of hazards should be treated as this project's principal risks?

options.text: Service strikes (the gas mains and the HV crossing), trench collapse and entry to unsupported ground, traffic incursion and plant/pedestrian conflict, the chamber atmosphere, and lifting pipes into the trench.
options.feedback: Correct. These are the credible fatal risks on a deep urban trench job, and each needs specific planning, exclusion rules and supervision — not generic controls.

options.text: Manual handling of pipe and fittings, slips and trips on spoil, vibration from breakers and abrasive wheel use — the accident data for utility gangs shows these cause most lost-time injuries, so they deserve the planning time.
options.feedback: Manage these too, but frequency is not severity. Your planning priority goes to the hazards that bury, electrocute, gas or crush.

options.text: The hazards in the groundworks contractor's own risk assessment — the trench is their workplace, they lay mains like this every week, their assessment was reviewed at tender and they know where the injuries come from.
options.feedback: The principal contractor plans, manages and coordinates the whole phase — including the traffic, public and utility interfaces no single contractor owns.
options.consequence: The contractor's assessment never covered the public interface; a pedestrian following an unsigned diversion stepped into the working lane and was clipped by a reversing dumper, suffering bruising.

options.text: Noise, dust, mud on the road, blocked driveways and lost parking — on a trading high street, public complaints are what get street works permits restricted or revoked.
options.feedback: Community impact matters and is worth planning, but it must never displace the fatal-risk planning that keeps your own people alive.
options.consequence: With planning effort on complaints, nobody set exclusion rules for the HV crossing; the excavator scraped the cable tiles before a banksman stopped it — a near miss that halted the run for a day.

steps.topic: Risk assessment — principal risks on utility works
steps.learningNote: Prioritise by severity and credibility: service strikes, collapse, traffic, confined spaces and lifting are the utility-sector killers. Spoil placement, dewatering and public protection then feed directly off those controls.

cppText.best: Principal risks: gas and HV service strikes; trench collapse / entry to unsupported excavation; live traffic incursion and plant-pedestrian conflict; confined space atmosphere in the deep chamber; lifting pipes over the open trench; spoil surcharge at the trench edge. Each carries specific RAMS, permits, exclusion rules and named supervision. Frequent-injury risks (manual handling, slips, cutting operations) controlled through task design, housekeeping and briefing.
cppText.partial: Main risks identified; traffic and utility interface risks need further coordination.
cppText.poor: Risk identification delegated to individual contractors.
cppText.unsafe: No structured hazard identification for the project.

riskEntry.hazard: Buried service strike / trench collapse / traffic incursion
riskEntry.control: Permit to dig with located services, progressive trench support, agreed TM with maintained safety zone, PC-coordinated RAMS and supervision

steps.prompt: The pipe is PE, jointed by fusion using heater plates and generators in the street — sometimes within metres of the gas main. Fuel is stored at the compound. What is your fire and ignition control approach?

options.text: Fusion and hot work under permit with gas monitoring near the main, fuel and generators separated at the compound with extinguishers, no smoking on the run, muster briefed, and the fire plan tied to the gas emergency procedure.
options.feedback: Correct. On this job the fire plan and the gas strike plan are two halves of one system — controlled ignition sources are what stand between a nicked gas service and an ignition.

options.text: Extinguishers on every vehicle and at each fusion position, a strict no-smoking rule along the whole run, fuel kept in a bunded, locked store at the compound, and fire points and the muster point covered at induction.
options.feedback: Necessary but nowhere near sufficient. The plan must control when and where ignition sources operate — especially fusion equipment near located gas plant.

options.text: Treat fusion as ordinary plant use rather than hot work — there's no flame or sparks — so set the heater plate and generator wherever suits each joint, then move them on to the next.
options.feedback: Heater plates run at over 200°C and generators spark. Near a gas main, 'not technically welding' is not a control measure.
options.consequence: A generator was run beside the trench next to an exposed gas service; the detector alarmed during a fusion joint and the gang evacuated — a near miss that stopped fusion work for a day.

options.text: Ban fusion in the street altogether and pre-fabricate every pipe string in the compound under a single hot works permit, towing finished strings out to the trench so no heater plate or generator ever runs near the gas main.
options.feedback: Pre-fabrication helps where practical, but 400 m of main needs in-trench connections regardless. An unworkable ban breeds uncontrolled workarounds — a permit system you can actually run is safer.
options.consequence: Towed strings blocked the live lane and tie-ins were still needed; a gang fused them in the trench without a permit or gas check, and a client audit found it and suspended fusion work.

steps.topic: Fire and ignition control near gas plant
steps.learningNote: Think fuel, ignition, people: control every ignition source (fusion kit, generators, cutting, smoking) with permits and gas monitoring where gas plant is nearby, keep fuel bunded and separated at the compound, and make the fire response and gas escape response one briefed system.

cppText.best: Fire plan: fusion jointing and hot work under permit with ignition control and gas monitoring within the exclusion distance of gas plant; generators and fuel at the compound — bunded, separated, extinguishers at the fire point; no smoking on the working lane; escape routes from the trench maintained (ladders at intervals); muster at compound with upwind alternative; gas escape procedure integrated with fire response and briefed at induction.
cppText.partial: Extinguishers and basic rules in place; permit control of fusion near gas plant to be implemented.
cppText.poor: Ignition sources uncontrolled along the working lane.
cppText.unsafe: Hot work/fusion carried out near gas plant with no ignition controls.

phases.title: RAMS Review
phases.intro: Method statements for trenching live or die on the details: support sequence, service avoidance, and who is allowed where.

steps.prompt: The groundworks contractor submits their RAMS for the main trench run. It describes 'excavation with suitable support as required' but doesn't state the trench box installation sequence, the service crossing controls or when operatives may enter. The gang is ready to start. Do you accept it?

options.text: Reject it with specific comments: require the dig-and-support sequence for the boxes, the rule that nobody enters ahead of installed support, controls at each service crossing, ladder positions and plant exclusion rules.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Support as required' is the phrase found in collapse investigations. If the RAMS can't tell you the sequence and the entry rule, it can't brief the gang.

options.text: Accept it on condition that the supervisor briefs the box sequence, the entry rule and the service crossing controls at the first toolbox talk, with the briefing signed by the gang and the written RAMS revised to match by the end of the week.
options.feedback: Verbal patches evaporate with the first crew change, and a signed briefing sheet is still not the method. The controlling document must carry the controls before work starts.

options.text: Accept it — the contractor lays mains on our framework every week, their method is well proven on this ground, and their accident record and insurance are both current and clean.
options.feedback: Experience without a defined method is exactly how experienced people die in trenches. Insurance pays out after the funeral.
options.consequence: With no written sequence, operatives went in to trim the face ahead of the box and a section of side slumped onto the bedding. Nobody was caught, but the run stopped while the RAMS was rewritten.

options.text: Let them start the first 50 m, where the trench is shallower and the records show no crossings, while the RAMS is revised with the box sequence, entry rule and service crossing controls for the deeper sections further along.
options.feedback: Ground doesn't read programmes, and records aren't the ground — even 'shallow' sections of this run pass live services. Starting work under a rejected method normalises exactly the behaviour that kills.
options.criticalFailure: Trenching started under inadequate RAMS
options.consequence: In the 'shallow' 50 m the gang dug ahead of the box to reach an unrecorded service; the face collapsed onto an operative's legs. He was hospitalised, it was RIDDOR-reported and HSE served a notice.

steps.topic: RAMS review — excavation and trench support
steps.learningNote: Test trenching RAMS against: what support, installed in what sequence, from where? When exactly may a person enter? What happens at each service crossing? Where are the ladders? If you can't picture the work hour by hour from the document, reject it.

phases.title: Temporary Works Register
phases.intro: Trench boxes, road plates, shaft support, thrust blocks — this job is temporary works from end to end. Appoint the coordinator, then set the right control level for each item.

steps.prompt: How is temporary works managed on this project?

options.text: Appoint a trained TWC in writing, keep a live register that moves with the works, check each box set-up against its tabulated data (design where it falls outside), and hold points: no entry before support sign-off, no traffic on plates before a permit to load.
options.feedback: Correct. On a linear job the register must move with the works — every re-set of a trench box in changed ground or next to the gas main is a fresh check, and the hold points are what keep people out of unproven excavations.

options.text: Let the groundworks foreman, with twenty years in trench support, set the boxes and stand-offs day by day — he reads changing ground faster than any register can be updated.
options.feedback: Ground-reading matters, but without a register, design limits and hold points, one optimistic morning is all it takes. The register is how the foreman's judgement gets checked, not replaced.
options.consequence: The foreman re-set a box in softer ground beyond its tabulated depth with no check; the box racked overnight and the bay had to be re-dug and re-supported, losing two shifts.

options.text: Put the bespoke items — chamber shaft, gas main support and thrust blocks — on the register with design checks, and manage the trench boxes as proprietary plant under the supplier's hire terms, user guide and tabulated data sheets.
options.feedback: Proprietary equipment used within its tabulated data is still temporary works — every box set-up goes on the register with its limits, checks against the actual depth, soil and surcharge, and inspections. The boxes are where most of this job's exposure sits.
options.consequence: Boxes were stacked beyond the supplier's data at a deeper dip with nobody checking; the supplier's engineer spotted it on a visit and the bay was closed for redesign and re-installation.

options.text: Keep the register and design checks current, but treat hold points as advisory on night shifts so the gang can reopen the lane on time without waiting for someone to sign off before entry or loading.
options.feedback: A register without enforced hold points is a diary of what you were going to check. The hold point before trench entry and before loading road plates is the control — and night shifts are when it matters most.
options.criticalFailure: Temporary works hold points removed under programme pressure
options.consequence: On a night shift a road plate was opened to traffic with no permit to load; it rocked off an unbedded edge and a car wheel dropped into the trench. The driver was hospitalised; RIDDOR-reported.

steps.topic: Temporary works — coordination on linear works
steps.learningNote: The TWC keeps the register live as the trench moves: box configurations checked against tabulated data for the actual depth, soil and surcharge; bespoke design where conditions fall outside it (deep chamber, alongside the gas main); and hold points at entry and loading that nobody bypasses.

cppText.best: Temporary Works Coordinator appointed in writing. Live TW register covers trench boxes, chamber shaft support, road plates, pedestrian trench crossings, thrust blocks, the gas main crossing support and the dewatering arrangement. Proprietary equipment verified against tabulated data for actual ground and surcharge; bespoke design with independent check for the chamber shaft and gas main sections. Hold points: no trench entry before support sign-off; permit to load before trafficking road plates.
cppText.partial: TW register established; verification of box configurations against tabulated data to be completed section by section.
cppText.poor: Temporary works managed informally by the groundworks foreman.
cppText.unsafe: Hold points removed — excavations entered and plates trafficked without sign-off.

steps.prompt: Work through the temporary works items identified for this project. For each, decide the controls that apply.

items.name: Trench boxes to main run (2.1 m deep)
items.description: Proprietary trench boxes installed by dig-and-push along the main run, used within the supplier's tabulated data for depth, soil type and surcharge.
items.explanation: Used within tabulated data this is a standard solution, but each set-up must be checked against the actual ground, depth and surcharge, inspected each shift, and no one enters until the supervisor signs the support off — that's the hold point.

items.name: Chamber connection shaft support (3.4 m deep)
items.description: Support to the deep excavation around the existing chamber, in mixed ground with the chamber wall as one face.
items.explanation: Deeper than the boxes' data, irregular geometry and an existing structure as one face — this is outside any standard solution. Bespoke design with an independent check, and a hold point before entry.

items.name: Excavation support alongside medium pressure gas main
items.description: Special support and controls where the trench runs immediately alongside and beneath the exposed gas main, including support to the exposed main itself.
items.explanation: An exposed, unsupported gas main is both a collapse and an explosion risk. The support to the excavation and to the main itself needs bespoke design, independent checking, utility company agreement, and a hold point before the main is undermined.

items.name: Road plates over open trench
items.description: Steel road plates spanning the trench at side roads and driveways so traffic can cross overnight.
items.explanation: Plates used within their rated span and bedded/secured per the standard details are a standard solution — but they carry the public's vehicles, so each installation is checked, and a permit to load is issued before traffic runs over them.

items.name: Pedestrian trench crossings / footbridges
items.description: Proprietary footbridge units with handrails where the diverted footway and shop accesses cross the open trench.
items.explanation: Proprietary units within their data, but they carry the public — including pushchairs and wheelchairs — so each placement is checked for bearing, fixing and edge protection before it opens, and inspected daily.

items.name: Temporary thrust restraint for pressure testing
items.description: Temporary thrust/anchor blocks restraining the main's end caps and bends during hydrostatic pressure testing.
items.explanation: Test pressures generate large thrust forces; a failed restraint launches fittings. Calculated, independently checked design and a hold point before the test — nobody in the trench near restrained ends while pressure is on.

items.name: Spoil placement control at trench edge
items.description: Managed rule for spoil heaps: minimum stand-off from the trench edge, heap height limits, contaminated spoil segregated on the lined area.
items.explanation: Not an engineered structure, but spoil surcharge changes the loading the boxes were checked against — so the stand-off rule is registered, briefed and inspected every shift rather than left to habit.

items.name: Dewatering pump and settlement arrangement
items.description: Sump pumps in the trench discharging through a settlement tank before controlled discharge, hoses routed clear of the footway.
items.explanation: A standard arrangement, but it belongs on the register: uncontrolled dewatering can draw fines out of the ground and undermine the trench sides and highway, so the set-up and discharge are checked daily.

items.name: Portable signals power supply
items.description: Battery/generator power arrangement for the portable traffic signals at each end of the works.
items.explanation: Not a structural temporary work — nothing is supported or retained. It is managed under the TM and electrical arrangements with daily checks, not on the TW register. Registers stay credible by holding what belongs on them.

steps.topic: Temporary works register — utility works
steps.learningNote: Everything that supports ground, carries load or restrains force goes on the register: boxes, shafts, plates, bridges, thrust blocks. Proprietary kit within tabulated data is a standard solution with checks; anything outside the data — deeper, odd geometry, next to the gas main — needs bespoke design with an independent check and a hold point.

phases.title: Permits and Inspections
phases.intro: Permits gate the tasks that can kill in one mistake; inspections prove the trench, the boxes and the TM are still what you signed off yesterday.

steps.prompt: Select the permit systems this project genuinely needs. Over-permitting buries supervisors in paperwork; under-permitting leaves lethal tasks uncontrolled.

options.name: Road / lane occupation (street works permit compliance)
Permit to load (road plates / temporary works)

steps.explanation: Every break of ground needs a permit to dig with located services; the chamber entry needs a confined space permit; occupation of each highway section is controlled against the street works permit conditions; road plates and other TW need a permit to load before traffic or plant runs over them; work near the HV crossing needs isolation/proximity control agreed with the network operator; and fusion jointing near gas plant is a controlled ignition source. There is no roofwork and no demolition in this scope — those permits would be paperwork without purpose.
steps.topic: Permit to work systems for street works
steps.learningNote: A permit is a formal pre-task check that the controls exist right now — located services, tested atmosphere, signed-off support — with a defined scope, duration and sign-back. Use permits where a single missed control is likely to be fatal, and keep the system lean enough to run properly on a moving site.

steps.prompt: Set the inspection regime for the project.

options.text: Excavations inspected by a competent person every shift start and after rain, flooding, strikes or loading; TM drive-through and walk-through checks at set times; plates and footbridges daily; lifting gear and detectors in date.
options.feedback: Correct. The statutory shift-start excavation inspection and post-event checks are the legal floor; TM, plates and detector checks are how a moving site catches deterioration before the public or the gang do.

options.text: A full recorded inspection of the excavation and boxes by the competent person every Monday, plus a visual by the gang each morning before they go in — it's the same trench, only longer each day.
options.feedback: Far outside the statutory frequency, and a glance by the gang isn't a recorded inspection. Every shift start, and after anything that could affect stability — a trench that moved 30 m since Monday is not 'the same trench'.
options.consequence: Midweek rain softened a bay that wasn't re-inspected; ground beneath a box slumped as the gang started work. Nobody was hurt, but the bay was re-dug and the client's audit raised it.

options.text: The statutory excavation inspections at every shift start and after bad weather, recorded by us; the TM crew, the plate and footbridge hirer and the lifting gear supplier each inspect and record their own equipment under their contracts.
options.feedback: Contractors check their own kit, but the PC must monitor the site as a whole. The TM layout and the public crossings are interfaces that fall between contractors unless you own them.

options.text: Brief the gangs to report anything that looks wrong straight away and give them authority to stop — they're in the trench all day and will spot cracks, water or a moving box long before a once-a-shift inspection, and the supervisor walks the run twice a day.
options.feedback: Reactive reporting finds the defect after it drops someone. Ground gives little visible warning before it lets go.
options.criticalFailure: No planned inspection regime for excavations and TM
options.consequence: A crack opening behind the end of the box line after overnight rain went unreported; the face fell onto an operative's legs. He was hospitalised, RIDDOR-reported, and HSE served an improvement notice.

steps.topic: Inspections — excavations, TM and equipment
steps.learningNote: Memorise the rhythm: excavations — start of every shift by a competent person, and after any event affecting stability; TM — after setting out, during the shift and after weather/interference, recorded; road plates and public crossings daily; gas detectors bump-tested and calibrated; lifting gear thoroughly examined and in date.

cppText.best: Inspection schedule: excavation and support inspected at the start of each shift and after rain, flooding, strikes or adjacent loading (recorded); TM drive-through/walk-through at start, mid and end of shift and after weather or interference; road plates and pedestrian footbridges checked daily and after trafficking; gas detectors bump-tested daily and calibrated to schedule; lifting accessories and excavator thorough-examination certificates verified; weekly recorded site manager inspection of the full run; actions tracked to closure.
cppText.partial: Statutory excavation inspections in place; TM and equipment checking to be formalised.
cppText.poor: Inspections limited to excavation only — TM and public interfaces unmonitored.

phases.title: High-Risk Activities
phases.intro: The chamber, the services and the lifts — control the work that can kill in a second.

steps.prompt: Sequence the work to excavate the 3.4 m connection shaft beside the medium-pressure gas main and then enter the existing chamber to make the connection.
steps.context: The shaft is in mixed ground with the chamber wall as one face, and the MP gas main runs along one edge at shallow depth. Support to the shaft and to the exposed main are both bespoke items on the TW register.

activities.label: Shaft and gas main support designs independently checked
activities.detail: Bespoke designs checked to the agreed category, gas network agreement on the main, hold points set.

activities.label: Records checked; CAT & Genny scan marks the services
activities.detail: MP gas main, HV and telecoms located and marked; records and scan compared and anomalies flagged.

activities.label: Permit to dig issued; trial holes hand-dug to the main
activities.detail: Insulated hand tools within the agreed distance; position and depth of the MP main positively proven.

activities.label: Support the exposed gas main before digging below it
activities.detail: Main supported and protected to the designed detail, witnessed by the gas network where required.

activities.label: Excavate in lifts, fitting support as each lift is dug
activities.detail: Nobody works below unsupported ground; spoil and plant kept back from the shaft edge.

activities.label: TWS inspects the support; hold point released
activities.detail: Completed support checked against the design and the permit to load/enter signed before work below.

activities.label: Atmosphere tested, ventilation on, rescue kit rigged
activities.detail: Calibrated monitor reading recorded; tripod and winch over the opening; top man and rescue team ready.

activities.label: Confined space permit issued; enter and monitor throughout
activities.detail: Entry team works to the permit with monitors worn; the top man controls entry and keeps contact.

constraints.reason: The main is supported to a designed, agreed detail — it can't be improvised once the main is hanging exposed.
Shaft support is installed to a checked design; digging first leaves the gang improvising support in a 3.4 m hole.
The permit to dig is issued on located, marked services, and the trial holes go where the scan points.
You can only support a main that has been exposed and positively identified by hand.
Machine excavation before trial holes have proven the main's position risks striking medium-pressure gas.
Digging below an unsupported gas main lets it sag or fracture, releasing gas into a deep, confined excavation.
The TWS inspects the completed support against the design — an inspection before installation proves nothing.
Nobody works at the bottom of the shaft or enters the chamber until the support hold point is released.
Entering before the atmosphere is tested and rescue is rigged leaves the team exposed with no way to be recovered.

steps.topic: High-risk sequencing — safe digging, BS 5975 hold points and confined space entry
steps.learningNote: Design and check the support before digging; locate, permit and trial-hole before any machine goes near the main; support the main before you undermine it; dig in lifts with support following so nobody stands below unsupported ground; release the TW hold point only after the TWS inspection; and enter the chamber only under a confined space permit with a tested atmosphere, continuous monitoring and rescue rigged.

steps.prompt: The connection into the existing 4 m deep chamber is due. How do you control the entry?

options.text: Treat it as a confined space: avoid entry if the connection can be made from outside; otherwise classify it, test before and monitor during entry, ventilate, and work to a permit with a trained top man, escape sets and rescue gear rigged before entry.
options.feedback: Correct. First ask whether the connection can be made without entry. If not: classified space, tested and monitored atmosphere, permit, top man, and rescue that works without waiting for the fire service.

options.text: Test the atmosphere with a calibrated four-gas monitor lowered on a line before entry; if it reads clear, the team works with the cover off for ventilation and a man stationed at the top.
options.feedback: Pre-entry testing is necessary but not sufficient: atmospheres change during work, especially when disturbing sediment and cutting into a live system. Continuous monitoring, a permit and rehearsed rescue arrangements are still required — a man at the top with no retrieval gear can only watch.

options.text: It's a clean-water chamber, not a sewer, so there's no gas risk — send the fitter down on a harness and line as a precaution and keep the cover off for fresh air while he works.
options.feedback: Oxygen depletion, ground gas and vapours occur in clean-water chambers too. A harness and line with no top man, no tested atmosphere and no retrieval gear is a recovery aid, not a rescue plan.
options.criticalFailure: Confined space entered without atmosphere testing or rescue arrangements
options.consequence: The fitter collapsed in oxygen-depleted air at the bottom of the chamber; with no top man or retrieval rig the fire service recovered him. He was hospitalised and HSE served a prohibition notice.

options.text: Use the quiet night shift so the chamber isn't blocked by daytime traffic, with the most experienced fitter making the entry, a four-gas monitor clipped to his chest, and his mate in the van nearby on the radio.
options.feedback: A personal monitor and a mate in the van on the radio are not a top man at the entry or a rescue plan. Night entry with reduced staffing removes rescue capability and supervision — experience does not metabolise a bad atmosphere.
options.consequence: During the night entry his monitor alarmed and he climbed out light-headed and unaided, while his mate in the van missed the radio call. Logged as a near miss; the client suspended chamber work.

steps.topic: Confined spaces — chamber entry
steps.learningNote: The Confined Spaces Regulations hierarchy: avoid entry if the work can be done from outside; if entry is unavoidable, work to a safe system — classification, atmosphere testing before and during, ventilation, permit, trained top man, communications, escape sets where specified, and rescue arrangements in place before entry that do not rely on the emergency services.

cppText.best: High-risk activities: confined space chamber entry avoided where possible; where required — classified, permit-controlled, atmosphere tested and continuously monitored, ventilated, trained top man, escape sets and rigged retrieval with rehearsed rescue plan. Trench entry only behind signed-off support. Safe digging around located services; no mechanical excavation within exclusion distances. Lifting under lift plans with exclusion zones; quick hitch checks enforced.
cppText.partial: Chamber entry controls defined; rescue rehearsal to be completed before entry.
cppText.poor: Chamber entry planned as routine work without classification.
cppText.unsafe: Confined space entry without tested atmosphere or rescue arrangements.

steps.prompt: The service plans show an HV cable crossing the trench line, position 'approximate'. The gang has a permit to dig for the section. How do they proceed at the crossing?

options.text: Locate with CAT and Genny from both sides, hand-dig trial holes with insulated tools to expose and identify the cable, agree protection and any isolation with the network operator, then dig mechanically outside the agreed distance, treating it as live.
options.feedback: Correct. Plans give you a search area, the locator gives you a signal, and only trial holes give you the truth. HV stays 'live until proven otherwise' even after the operator quotes an isolation.

options.text: Sweep with the CAT, mark the strongest signal, then take the excavator across in shallow scrapes with a banksman watching the teeth for marker tape or cable tiles.
options.feedback: A locator signal is not a position — depth and lateral error are routine, and HV strikes kill operators and anyone touching the machine. Mechanical excavation over an unproven HV cable is the classic fatal shortcut.
options.criticalFailure: Mechanical excavation over unproven HV cable
options.consequence: The cable lay 400 mm off the marked line; the bucket struck it and the flash burned the banksman's hand. The strike was reported as a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence and HSE investigated.

options.text: The record puts the cable half a metre below formation and the CAT reading agrees it's deep, so brief the operator on its position, have a banksman watch for marker tape or cable tiles, and dig the crossing in the normal way with a toothless ditching bucket.
options.feedback: Recorded depths are unreliable — roads get regraded and cables rise and dip — and locator depth readings are estimates, not proof. Marker tape is frequently missing, and by the time the operator sees it the bucket is already there.
options.consequence: The cable was 300 mm higher than recorded; the bucket cracked its tile cover before the banksman shouted. A near miss that cost a day while the network operator inspected the cable.

options.text: Hand-dig the full 20 m either side of the drawn position with insulated tools, since the record is only approximate and the locator can be misled by the ducts and gas main nearby, and bring the excavator back only once the cable is found.
options.feedback: Safe but unfocused — locating and trial holes narrow the hand-dig zone to where it's needed. Safe digging practice is targeted, not exhausting.

steps.topic: Buried services — safe digging near HV
steps.learningNote: The safe digging sequence: obtain plans, locate and mark with CAT and genny, permit to dig, trial holes by hand with insulated tools to positively identify, then controlled digging respecting exclusion distances — with services supported and protected once exposed, and everything treated as live until the owner proves otherwise.

riskEntry.hazard: HV cable crossing the trench line — position approximate
riskEntry.control: Located, trial-holed and positively identified; network operator agreement; exclusion distance for mechanical digging; cable supported, protected and treated as live

steps.prompt: Pipes are lifted from the laydown area and lowered into the trench by the excavator. Mid-morning you see a chain sling wrapped around a pipe, an operative steadying it from inside the trench, and the quick hitch pin check missing from the daily record. What is the standard you enforce?

options.text: Stop the lift. Lifts are planned, with certified accessories and a pipe-lifting attachment; tag lines control the load from outside the trench; nobody is in the trench or under the load; and the quick hitch check is recorded daily.
options.feedback: Correct. An excavator lifting is a lifting operation under LOLER — plan, certified gear, exclusion below the load. Detached quick hitch buckets and dropped pipes kill people standing exactly where that operative was.

options.text: Let this pipe land, since stopping a suspended load mid-swing carries its own risk, then stop the gang, swap the chain for a rated pipe sling, and brief the hitch check and the exclusion rule before the next lift goes up.
options.feedback: The riskiest seconds are the landing, with the man in the trench under a suspended load. Stopping means holding the load steady and getting him out first — 'after this one' is how supervisors describe the lift that dropped.
options.consequence: As the pipe landed it swung and trapped the operative's hand against the trench box; he needed hospital treatment for a crushed finger, and the client raised a lifting non-conformance.

options.text: Stop the lift and take the excavator off pipe lifting for the rest of the job — bring in a lorry loader with a trained operator and a slinger working outside the trench, so lifting becomes a separate, planned operation with its own lift plan and certified gear.
options.feedback: Excavators may lift when rated, examined and planned for it — that's what the machine is there for. Swapping plant doesn't fix the real failures: the sling, the man in the trench and the missing hitch check.

options.text: Let the gang carry on — guiding pipes in by hand is how mains have always been laid, the sling is rated for the weight, and the hitch was checked when the machine arrived on hire.
options.feedback: Normalised deviation. Quick hitch failures happen between hire checks, and 'always done it' is the phrase in the incident report after the pipe swings or drops.
options.criticalFailure: Operative under suspended load with unverified quick hitch
options.consequence: The unchecked quick hitch later released the bucket mid-slew and it dropped into the trench a metre from an operative. It was a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence and HSE served an improvement notice.

steps.topic: Lifting operations and the people–plant interface
steps.learningNote: Excavator lifting comes under LOLER: planned lifts, rated machine, certified accessories, thorough examinations in date. Control the interface: exclusion zone in the slew radius, tag lines from outside the trench, nobody below a suspended load, and a recorded daily quick hitch engagement check — most hitch failures are latch/pin errors on the day, not manufacturing faults.

phases.title: Environmental Management
phases.intro: Everything you pump, spill or stockpile on this street is a few metres from a gully that feeds a watercourse. Control it before it moves.

steps.prompt: Set the environmental controls for the project — the trench needs dewatering, spoil is stockpiled and hauled off, plant refuels near the works, and part of the run smells of hydrocarbons from an old garage site.

options.text: Pump through a settlement tank to an agreed, consented discharge; protect gullies; test and segregate the suspect spoil on a lined area with covered haulage and duty-of-care notes; refuel on drip trays away from gullies; inform residents.
options.feedback: Correct. Silt is a pollutant, dewatering needs a lawful discharge route, and contaminated spoil handled as clean waste is both an offence and a health exposure. Neighbour goodwill on a high street is programme protection.

options.text: Pump trench water to the nearest gully through a filter sock so the silt stays in the trench, and blend the hydrocarbon-smelling spoil through the main stockpile so that no single load fails the tip's acceptance testing.
options.feedback: A sock does not treat silty water, and deliberately diluting contaminated spoil to disguise it is a waste offence, not a workaround.
