options.criticalFailure: Silty dewatering discharge to gully and deliberate dilution of contaminated spoil
options.consequence: Silty, oily water from the gully reached the local brook; the Environment Agency traced it to the works and served an enforcement notice, and the blended spoil was rejected at the tip.

options.text: Start dewatering and muck-away to the usual tip now, then settle the discharge consent and waste classification at the end once the real volumes and test results are known.
options.feedback: Duty of care and discharge consents apply from the first load and the first pump-out, not retrospectively. Trenching is the highest-pollution-risk stage of the whole project.
options.consequence: Suspect spoil went to the inert tip unclassified; the tip rejected the loads after a sample failed, and the client paid to recover and reclassify them while muck-away stood for two days.

options.text: Tanker all trench water to a licensed treatment works and send every load of spoil, clean or not, to a licensed hazardous waste facility, whatever it costs, so no part of the job depends on test results, a discharge consent or a stockpile.
options.feedback: Lawful and safe, but settlement and testing would show most of it can be managed locally at a fraction of the cost — proportionate control beats blanket disposal.

steps.topic: Environmental controls — dewatering, silt, spoil and spills
steps.learningNote: Know where every gully leads before you pump anything. Dewatering goes through settlement to an agreed, consented discharge point; suspect spoil gets tested and segregated before it's classified and hauled under duty-of-care paperwork; refuelling gets drip trays, spill kits and distance from drains; and the community gets told what's happening before they smell or hear it.

cppText.best: Environmental controls: dewatering via settlement tank to agreed consented discharge point — no direct discharge to gullies; gully protection along the working lane; suspect spoil tested, segregated on lined area, hauled covered by licensed carriers with waste documentation retained; refuelling with drip trays and spill kits away from gullies; noise and working hours per permit conditions; resident and shop communication with complaints log.
cppText.partial: Basic silt and waste controls in place; discharge consent and spoil testing to be confirmed.
cppText.poor: Environmental controls deferred until quantities known.
cppText.unsafe: Silty water discharged to gully; contaminated spoil diluted into clean stockpile.

phases.title: Incident / Challenge Events
phases.intro: The street will test you. Respond to what it throws at you — your judgement under pressure is what's being assessed.

steps.prompt: EVENT: The banksman shouts up — there's a strong smell of gas in the trench near the exposed low pressure main. No visible damage, no alarm on the detector yet.

options.text: Get everyone out and upwind, kill ignition sources including plant and fusion kit, cordon off and move the public back, call the gas emergency number, and stay out until the network confirms it's safe. Then review the cause and report.
options.feedback: Correct. Smell beats the detector — trust it. Evacuate, remove ignition, cordon wide (including shoppers and traffic), call it in, and stay out. If the works caused a gas escape, that's a reportable dangerous occurrence.

options.text: Send the banksman, who carries the gas detector and is trained in its use, back down briefly to trace the source along the exposed main, so you can give the emergency line an exact location and save their engineer valuable time finding it.
options.feedback: You've just sent someone into a potentially explosive atmosphere in a trench with limited escape. The gas network locates leaks — that's their emergency service.
options.criticalFailure: Operative sent into suspected gas atmosphere to investigate
options.consequence: The banksman became dizzy at the leak and two colleagues climbed in to help him out; all three were checked at hospital, the escape was reported as a dangerous occurrence and HSE investigated.

options.text: Ventilate the bay with the compressor airline for ten minutes to disperse any build-up, keep the plant switched off, then resume once the detector stays clear and the smell fades.
options.feedback: You may be moving a flammable mixture around rather than removing the leak — and compressed air kit is itself an ignition risk. The escape is still escaping.
options.consequence: The airline pushed gas along the trench toward a running generator at the next fusion position; it was shut down just before the detector alarmed there. A near miss, and the works stopped for a day.

options.text: Clear that bay, shut down the plant there and call the gas emergency number, but keep the rest of the run working while you wait — the smell is localised, the detector is silent and the next working bay is 50 m further along the street.
options.feedback: Gas travels along the trench and through ground and ducts. The cordon and stand-down must reflect where gas could reach, not where the nose first caught it — including the ignition sources in the other bays.

steps.topic: Gas escape response
steps.learningNote: Gas smell in an excavation: evacuate and cordon (people, public, traffic), eliminate ignition sources, call the gas emergency line, no re-entry until the network operator declares it safe. A gas escape caused by the works is a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence — report it, then fix the system that let it happen.

steps.prompt: EVENT: A resident, furious about access, has dragged two barriers and a run of cones aside to drive out of his driveway — leaving a gap in the guarding two metres from the open trench, with school pick-up in an hour.

options.text: Reinstate the guarding now, then deal with the cause: visit the resident, agree managed access (a plated crossing or escorted exits at set times), brief the gang and TM crew, and add driveway accesses to the TM checks and resident communications.
options.feedback: Correct. Make the physical protection whole first, then remove the reason it keeps being breached. Residents defeated your guarding once; they'll do it nightly unless access is genuinely solved.

options.text: Put the barriers back straight away and report the resident to the police and the highway authority for interfering with street works, so there's a formal record and an officer can warn him before he does it again.
options.feedback: Reinstating is right, and interference can be an offence — but leading with enforcement against a resident you've boxed in escalates the conflict and doesn't fix the access problem that caused it.

options.text: Put a cone across the gap until the end of the shift — he'll only drag the barriers again on his way home — and re-fix the full guarding before the gang leaves tonight.
options.feedback: A cone is not guarding. That leaves an open gap next to a 2.1 m trench, an hour before children walk past — precisely the scenario trench guarding exists to prevent.
options.criticalFailure: Gap in trench guarding left open on the public footway
options.consequence: During school pick-up a child ran through the coned gap and fell into the trench, breaking an arm. The incident was RIDDOR-reported, HSE investigated and the authority suspended the permit.

options.text: Chain and clamp the barriers so they can't be moved again, and post a letter through his door explaining that interfering with street works guarding is a criminal offence.
options.feedback: You've now trapped a resident's vehicle and guaranteed a nastier confrontation — and determined people defeat chained barriers. Solve access, don't harden the standoff.
options.consequence: The resident cut the chain to get to work and left the barrier lying across the footway, where a pedestrian tripped over it; he then complained to the client and the local councillor.

steps.topic: TM interference and third-party access
steps.learningNote: Treat every interference with guarding as a system warning, not just a breach: reinstate immediately, find out why it happened, and design the reason away — plated accesses, escorted movements, timed arrangements. Communication with frontagers before you close their access prevents most of these events.

phases.title: Progress Review
phases.intro: Mid-project: the authority, the client and the community all want things faster. Hold the standards while you hold the relationships.

steps.prompt: The highway authority asks you to give the lane back for the weekend street market — two days early. The trench in that section is laid but not backfilled and compacted. The agent suggests 'whip the TM off Friday night, cone just the trench line'. Your response?

options.text: Re-plan: resource the backfill and interim reinstatement to finish that section Friday, or plate it under a permit to load with reduced but compliant guarding, and agree the revised occupation with the authority. The lane goes back only when safe.
options.feedback: Correct. There are two safe ways to give the lane back — finish it or plate it under TW control — and one unsafe way. Handled well, the market weekend becomes the moment the authority starts trusting you.

options.text: Agree, take the full TM off Friday night as the agent suggests, and run a continuous line of cones and tape along the open trench — it's two days, and the market is mostly on foot.
options.feedback: Market crowds, an open or soft trench line, and cones instead of guarding. This is how pedestrians and unbraced excavations meet.
options.criticalFailure: TM and guarding stripped from unfinished excavation for a public event
options.consequence: At dusk a shopper pushing a buggy stepped through the cone line and fell into the open trench, fracturing a wrist; the authority suspended the permit and HSE investigated the guarding.

options.text: Decline in writing — the agreed permit runs to Sunday, the trench isn't ready, and changing a live TM layout at short notice carries its own risk for the TM crew and the gang.
options.feedback: You're entitled to your dates, but a refusal with no alternative wastes an opportunity and sours the relationship that every future permit variation depends on. Engage with a safe option.
options.consequence: The authority later refused the client's early-start variation for the next section, citing the market refusal, and the programme lost several days of occupation.

options.text: Keep the gang on through Friday night to backfill and compact the section, with a tower light, the night foreman and a hired roller, so the lane can be handed back to the authority first thing Saturday morning as it asked.
options.feedback: Rushed, fatigued, unplanned night work produces poor compaction you'll be digging up again — and tired people around plant in the dark. Plan the acceleration or plate the trench.

steps.topic: Programme pressure — early handback
steps.learningNote: When pressed to give road space back early: accelerate with a plan, or bridge the gap with engineered temporary works (plates under permit to load, compliant guarding) — never by de-controlling. The permit conditions can be varied by agreement; safety standards can't.

steps.prompt: The section past the school crossing must be done at night over four shifts. How do you set this night working up?

options.text: Brief the night gang on layout, hazards and emergency plans before shift one; letter-drop residents and the school; light without glare; keep noise to agreed hours; manage fatigue; hand the crossing back plated or reinstated before school.
options.feedback: Correct. Night works succeed on communication in both directions: a properly briefed gang working in good light, and a community that knew it was coming — with the crossing handed back safe before the first child arrives.

options.text: Run the nights under the day RAMS and CPP, with tower lights on each bay, the same supervisor and the same emergency arrangements — the work itself doesn't change after dark.
options.feedback: Night changes the risk profile: visibility, fatigue, lone-ness, drunk drivers, and no passing supervision. One light and daytime paperwork doesn't cover it — and nobody told the school.

options.text: Tell the school, but keep resident notice to a minimum — a letter-drop well ahead only generates objections, and most of the noisy breaking will be finished before midnight.
options.feedback: They'll find out at 11pm through the bedroom window, and the complaints will land on the authority that grants your permits. Communication is a permit condition on most night works anyway.
options.consequence: Residents woken by the breaker on the first night complained to the councillor and the authority; a midnight cut-off was imposed and the crossing section overran by a night.

options.text: Run the four nights with the day gang on overtime — they know this street, its services and the TM layout far better than a fresh night crew would after a single briefing, and familiar faces will reassure the school and the residents on the parade.
options.feedback: Twelve dark hours after eight daylight ones puts exhausted people next to live traffic and an open trench. Familiarity doesn't survive fatigue.
options.consequence: Late on the third night a fatigued operative reversed a dumper into the barrier line at the crossing; nobody was hurt, but the near miss was investigated and the client demanded a new shift pattern.

steps.topic: Night working and community communication
steps.learningNote: Night working needs its own plan: task lighting without glare, briefed emergency arrangements, fatigue-managed shift patterns, noise controls, and proactive communication with residents, the school and the authority. Handing back the school crossing safe before each morning is a hard hold point, not an aspiration.

cppText.best: Communication arrangements: induction for all including night gang; daily pre-start briefings at the works; task-specific RAMS briefings before each new activity; letter drops and notice boards for residents and shops with 24-hour contact number; school and crossing patrol liaison for the night working section; highway authority coordination meetings; complaints log reviewed weekly; F10 and permits displayed at the compound.
cppText.partial: Workforce briefing in place; resident and school communication to be formalised before night works.
cppText.poor: Communication reactive — community learns of works when they start.
cppText.unsafe: Night works commenced with no briefing or community notification.

phases.title: Handover
phases.intro: A street works job isn't finished when the water flows — it's finished when the highway authority accepts the road back and the records protect the next person who digs here.

steps.prompt: The main is commissioned. What does a proper close-out require?

options.text: Permanent reinstatement to specification with compaction and material records, completion registered so the guarantee starts, TM removed in reverse order, and as-laid line, depth, materials and residual risks handed over.
options.feedback: Correct. Reinstatement is a specified, guaranteed product with a defects liability on you — and the as-laid records are what stop the next contractor's CAT survey being a work of fiction over your main.

options.text: Complete interim reinstatement throughout, register it with the authority and keep it inspected, remove the TM in reverse order, and programme the permanent surfacing for whenever the reinstatement subcontractor next has a gang free.
options.feedback: Interim reinstatement is legitimate — but it has a time limit, it must be registered and maintained, and 'when a gang is free' is how interim patches fail, trip pedestrians and draw authority defect notices.

options.text: Backfill with the remaining excavated spoil, run the plate over it a couple of times, then lay the surface course — the authority's coring mostly checks the surfacing thickness.
options.feedback: Unspecified backfill and no compaction control gives you settlement over a live main under a live road — coring will find it, the authority will fail it, and you'll dig it all up again at your cost.
options.criticalFailure: Reinstatement carried out with uncontrolled materials and no compaction records
options.consequence: The trench settled under traffic over the new main; a cyclist came off at the dip and was hospitalised, and the authority's coring failed the reinstatement, forcing re-excavation at the contractor's cost.

options.text: Finish reinstatement and remove the TM, then have the surveyor compile the as-laid drawings next month from his set-out data, photos and the gang's daily sheets, as he does on every Midshire job, so the file is complete in one go.
options.feedback: Records assembled after demobilisation are incomplete records. Capture depths, materials and positions as each section closes — the file is built progressively or it's built wrong.
options.consequence: The health and safety file reached the client incomplete; the client withheld retention until as-laid depths were re-surveyed at the service crossings, at the contractor's cost.

steps.topic: Reinstatement and handover
steps.learningNote: Reinstatement to highway standards is a specified product: materials, layers, compaction, testing, with registration to the authority and a guarantee period. Handover also means the safety information: as-laid line and depth, materials, chamber details and residual risks into the health and safety file — the protection for whoever digs this street next.

cppText.best: Handover: permanent reinstatement to highway standards with material and compaction records; completion registered with the highway authority and guarantee period tracked; TM removed in the planned reverse sequence; as-laid records (line, depth, materials, chambers, residual risks) provided to the client and Principal Designer for the health and safety file; compound reinstated and car park returned; defects contact arrangements in place.
cppText.partial: Interim reinstatement registered with programme for permanent works; records partially assembled.
cppText.poor: Reinstatement complete but records and registration outstanding.
cppText.unsafe: Reinstatement uncontrolled — no material or compaction records.

phases.title: Final Score and Feedback
phases.intro: Works complete, road handed back. Review your performance across every discipline.

steps.title: Road handed back
body: The new main is live, the reinstatement is registered and the high street is trading normally over your trench line.

Your decisions through 16 weeks of street works planning, buried services, trench support, confined space work, traffic management and reinstatement have been assessed across legal compliance, safety control, planning, temporary works, environment, programme and quality.
Continue to your score report, Construction Phase Plan, registers and trackers — and see how your street works site set-up compared with the model answer.
keyPoints: Review your missed items report — those are your revision topics
Download your CPP, TW register and permit selections for tutor discussion
Try the scenario again and beat your grade

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: A loud bang and flash from the trench — the excavator has clipped the HV cable outside the trial-holed section. The operator is unhurt and still in the cab. The bucket is near the cable.

options.text: Keep everyone clear; tell the operator to stay in the cab unless fire forces him out (then jump clear, never touching machine and ground together); cordon off, call the network operator, treat it as live, report and investigate.
options.feedback: Correct. The ground and machine may be energised — the cab is the safest place until the network operator makes it dead. A struck HV cable is a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence, and the real finding is why the permit-to-dig boundary was crossed.

options.text: Have the operator raise the bucket slowly clear of the cable and track back a few metres, so the machine is no longer in contact if the circuit is re-energised.
options.feedback: Moving the machine risks re-striking or dragging the damaged cable and re-arcing. Nothing moves until the cable is confirmed dead.
options.consequence: As the bucket lifted it dragged the damaged cable, which re-arced; the operator was shaken but unhurt. The network operator extended the outage and the investigation criticised the response.

options.text: The protection has tripped, so the cable is dead for now — photograph the damage, cone off the bay and report it to the network operator, then carry on in the next bay, well away from the strike, while their engineer is on his way.
options.feedback: HV networks re-energise automatically — 'it tripped' can mean 'it's about to try again'. Working next to a damaged HV cable that hasn't been proven dead is a fatality risk, and a strike is also a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence, not just a network report.
options.criticalFailure: Work continued adjacent to damaged HV cable without confirmation it was dead
options.consequence: The circuit auto-reclosed while an operative hand-dug in the next bay a metre from the cable; the flash burned his arm. HSE found the strike had not been reported as a dangerous occurrence and served a notice.

options.text: Get the operator out of the cab and well away immediately — machines can catch fire after a strike and the cab is where he's most exposed — then cordon the area, keep the public back and call the network operator's emergency line.
options.feedback: Right instinct about fire, wrong default: with no fire, the cab is safer than stepping onto potentially energised ground. Evacuating the cab is the exception with its own technique, not the first move.

eventPool.learningNote: On an HV strike: people clear, operator stays in the cab unless fire (then jump clear, feet together, never touching machine and ground at once), cordon, network operator emergency line, treat as live until formally made dead. Report the dangerous occurrence, then investigate the permit and locating failure that let the bucket get there.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: You arrive at the head of the trench as the excavator starts to lift a trench box forward to the next bay — with an operative still in the trench between the box and the face, finishing bedding.

options.text: Stop the lift, get the operative out by the ladder before anything moves, then reset the rule with the gang: nobody in the trench while boxes are lifted, moved or pulled, with a head-count and banksman–operator confirmation before every move.
options.feedback: Correct. A suspended box over a person in a trench combines a dropped-load hazard with an unsupported face. Stop, extract the person, then fix the communication failure that let the lift start.

options.text: Let the operator complete the move slowly with the banksman guiding, while the operative stands still against the laid pipe, well away from the chains and the box, then climbs out once it lands.
options.feedback: There is nowhere safe to stand in a trench under a suspended trench box beside a face the box no longer supports. 'Slowly' does not change the physics.
options.criticalFailure: Trench box moved with operative still in the excavation
options.consequence: As the box lifted, the unsupported face behind it slumped onto the operative's legs and pinned him against the pipe. He suffered a fractured leg; RIDDOR-reported, and HSE served a prohibition notice.

options.text: Stop the lift, get the operative out by the ladder, and give the banksman a written warning on the spot in front of the gang, so everyone sees that a box move with someone still below will not be tolerated on this job.
options.feedback: Stopping is right, but instant blame before investigation misses the system question — was there ever an agreed exclusion-and-headcount procedure for box moves, and did the RAMS state it?

options.text: Let it go this time and raise it at tomorrow's briefing — the operative was well clear of the chains, the box was moving away from him, and the gang is behind programme.
options.feedback: Waiting for tomorrow's briefing means walking past it today — and what you walk past is the new standard. Next time the operative will be under the box, and everyone will remember the manager who watched.
options.consequence: On a later move the same operative was in the trench as a box swung forward; the banksman's shout got him clear. A visiting client auditor saw it and escalated the near miss.

eventPool.learningNote: Trench boxes are moved with the excavation empty of people: agreed sequence, positive communication between banksman and operator, head-count before every lift, and ladder access positioned so getting out is always quick. The moment support moves, the trench is unsupported — treat every box move like a fresh excavation.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: At 3:20pm a parent reports that a child squeezed through a gap where two pedestrian barriers meet near the school crossing and was steps from the trench edge before being grabbed.

options.text: Make the guarding continuous now — interlocked barriers, no gaps a child fits through — then treat it as a near miss: walk the route at child height, brief the gang and TM crew, check before school times, and tell the school.
options.feedback: Correct. Fix the gap, then fix the class of failure — every joint and pinch point along 400 m, checked at the times children are actually there. Closing the loop with the school turns a frightening moment into visible competence.

options.text: Close the gap with an extra barrier, thank the parent, then remind the TM crew to watch the joints near the school — it was one gap on one day, and nobody was hurt.
options.feedback: You fixed one gap out of dozens of barrier joints on a moving site. Without a systematic check, the same event repeats at the next joint — perhaps without the grab.
options.consequence: A toddler later slipped through another unlinked joint further along and was caught by a shopkeeper; the parent complained to the client and the authority inspected the guarding.

options.text: Close the gap now and post an operative as a dedicated guard at the crossing during school arrival and pick-up for the rest of the job, so a person is always watching the most exposed stretch rather than relying on barrier joints alone.
options.feedback: A person at school times can be part of the answer, but people look away and go on breaks — physical continuity of guarding is the control; supervision supplements it.

options.text: Ask the head teacher to write to parents asking that children use the far footway until the job finishes, put signs at the school gate directing families to that side, and ask the crossing patrol to hold children there at arrival and pick-up.
options.feedback: You can't delegate your guarding duty to teachers and parents, and rerouting children across a live road may add risk rather than remove it. Your barriers must work regardless of anyone else's behaviour.
options.consequence: Children sent to the far footway crossed between parked cars on the live road; the crossing patrol reported a near miss with a van, and the school complained to the client.

eventPool.topic: Public protection — children at street works
eventPool.learningNote: Children are foreseeably drawn to street works, and the law and every authority expect guarding that a child cannot defeat: continuous, interlocked, gap-free barriers with trench covers where needed. Near misses with children get the full treatment — systematic fix, timed checks, school liaison — because the next one may not be a near miss.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: The portable signals fail at 8am — both heads dark, traffic backing up in both directions, horns going. The foreman offers to 'wave traffic through' while an operative reboots the controller.

options.text: No hand-waving of live traffic. Trained TM operatives put in the agreed fallback (stop/go boards or manual control from safe positions), the TM contractor is called, signal-dependent work pauses, and the authority is told.
options.feedback: Correct. Directing live traffic is a trained task with proper equipment and positions — an improvising foreman in the carriageway is a casualty waiting for a distracted driver. The fallback should have been in the TM plan before the signals ever went out.

options.text: Let the foreman marshal the traffic with a stop/go board until the reboot — he's got twenty years on the roads, a high-vis coat and a clear view of both queues.
options.feedback: Untrained traffic direction in a live carriageway, in rush hour, with frustrated drivers. Vests don't stop cars, and his twenty years were spent behind guarding, not in front of it.
options.criticalFailure: Untrained person directing live traffic in the carriageway
options.consequence: A driver misread the foreman's board and moved off toward him; he was knocked down and fractured a wrist. It was RIDDOR-reported and the authority required a TM review before works resumed.

options.text: Switch the heads off, open both directions to free flow and let drivers give way to each other past the works — the trench is coned and barriered, the street is straight with clear sight lines both ways, and it's only until the controller reboots.
options.feedback: Two-way traffic through a single lane with no priority control produces head-on conflicts beside your workforce. The cones guard the trench, not the oncoming traffic.
options.consequence: Two cars met head-on alongside the works and one mounted the kerb into the coned area; nobody was hurt, but the near miss and the queues brought a formal complaint from the authority.

options.text: Stop all work, get the gang out of the working area and close the road completely with the TM crew's barriers until the signal engineer arrives, then reopen under the signals once they've been tested — whatever the queues do in the meantime.
options.feedback: Safe for your gang, but an unplanned full closure of a high street without authority agreement causes chaos and may breach your permit. The planned fallback exists so you don't have to choose between unsafe and shut.

eventPool.learningNote: Every signals installation needs a planned fallback: qualified manual control or stop/go operation, safe operator positions, and a repair call-out route. Only trained TM operatives control live traffic. If the fallback can't be sustained, the works that rely on that protection stop, and the authority is told.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: After overnight storms, 40 m of trench is flooded to knee depth and one trench box has visibly dropped at a corner where the bedding has washed out. The gang wants to pump out and get back in — pipes are due at 9am.

options.text: Nobody enters. Pump down through the settlement tank, then have the trench, boxes and their bearing inspected before re-entry, with the dropped box reset from above and the TWS involved. The pipes wait for the inspection.
options.feedback: Correct. Flooding is precisely the 'event affecting stability' that triggers a fresh inspection — washed-out bedding means the box may no longer be supported by what it was checked against. Silty pump-out water still goes through settlement.

options.text: Pump at full rate and let the gang follow the falling water down to re-bed the dropped corner by hand, so the bay is ready for the 9am pipe delivery.
options.feedback: Softened, undermined ground and a dropped box, with people back in before anyone competent has looked at it. Saturated trenches collapse after the water leaves, not just while it's there.
options.criticalFailure: Re-entry to flooded excavation before post-event inspection
options.consequence: As the water fell the softened face beside the dropped box slumped, burying an operative to the waist; he was freed with leg injuries, it was RIDDOR-reported and HSE served a prohibition notice.

options.text: Pump straight to the nearest gully — it's storm rainwater, not trench spoil — so the settlement tank isn't a bottleneck, and have the bay inspected before re-entry once it's drained.
options.feedback: It went in as rainwater; it's coming out as silt-laden trench water. Straight to the gully is a pollution incident on top of your flood.
options.consequence: Silty water from the gully discoloured the local brook; a resident reported it, the Environment Agency visited and the client received a warning letter demanding a written clean-up plan.

options.text: Fence off the flooded 40 m and leave it for two days to drain down naturally, and open a new dig further along the run, outside the flooded length, so the gang and the 9am pipe delivery stay productive in the meantime.
options.feedback: Cautious, but it leaves a compromised, water-filled excavation unassessed on a public street and doubles your open trench. Inspect, make safe and recover the section — that's what the post-event inspection is for.

eventPool.learningNote: After flooding, rain, a strike or adjacent loading: no entry until a competent person has inspected the excavation and its support. Washed-out bedding changes what the boxes are standing on. Pump-out water is silty water — it goes through settlement, never straight to the gully.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: A new gang started this morning at the far end of the run. On your walk you find their spoil heaped hard against the trench edge, high side toward the excavation, with the boxes below carrying load they weren't checked for.

options.text: Stop the bay, get everyone out, pull the spoil back to the stand-off with the machine and re-inspect the support before re-entry; then fix the cause — the new gang was never briefed: induct them and check their other bays.
options.feedback: Correct. Spoil surcharge at the edge loads the ground and the boxes beyond what was checked and can push the face in below. Clear it, re-inspect, then close the induction gap that caused it — and assume they've done it everywhere they've worked.

options.text: Have the gang take the top off the heap so it's below the barrier line, carry on with the bay, and cover the stand-off rule with the new starters at Friday's toolbox talk.
options.feedback: Cosmetic trimming leaves surcharge at the edge for four more days while the gang keeps working below it. The load is the problem, not the silhouette.
options.consequence: The remaining surcharge pushed a box out of line overnight; the next shift found a gap opening behind it and the bay had to be re-dug and re-supported, losing a day.

options.text: Phone the groundworks contractor's supervisor and leave it with him to sort — it's their gang, their trench, their spoil rule and their RAMS, he knows the new starters, and he's due back on site this afternoon anyway.
options.feedback: The PC coordinates and monitors the whole site. Walking past a loaded trench edge with people below it is an abdication that an investigation would quote back to you.
options.criticalFailure: Spoil surcharge against trench edge left uncorrected with operatives below
options.consequence: Before the supervisor arrived the surcharged edge sheared and spoil slid over the box onto an operative's shoulder. He was hospitalised; RIDDOR-reported, and HSE served an improvement notice.

options.text: Stop the bay, get the gang out and clear the spoil, then change the method for the rest of the job: every bucket loads straight to a waiting wagon, with no stockpiling anywhere along the run, so the edge can never be surcharged again.
options.feedback: It removes the hazard but at heavy cost and lorry movements the street doesn't need. The stand-off rule works — the failure was briefing, not the concept of a stockpile.

eventPool.topic: Spoil management — surcharge at the excavation edge
eventPool.learningNote: Spoil, materials and plant are kept back from the excavation edge — the stand-off in your RAMS and TW checks exists because surcharge loads the face and the support. New gangs are where rules quietly die: brief them before their first shift and inspect their first day's work.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: A highway authority street works inspector visits and finds your works 60 m beyond the extent noticed on the current permit — the trench progressed faster than the paperwork. He's writing it up now.

options.text: Acknowledge it and cooperate; regularise now — vary the permit for the actual extent and hold the head of the works within the permitted length until it's granted — then fix the process so progress is checked against the permit daily.
options.feedback: Correct. Take the finding, stop compounding it, and repair the coordination the noticing system exists for — it protects other works, bus routes and emergency plans. Handled openly, one defect notice needn't poison the relationship.

options.text: Explain to the inspector that the line and total length were on the original application, so the extra 60 m is a timing technicality he could reasonably waive.
options.feedback: The permit extent is the legal basis of your occupation, not a technicality. Arguing with the inspector converts a fixable defect into a hostile file.
options.consequence: The inspector recorded the argument in his report; the authority issued a fixed penalty and placed the works on an enhanced inspection regime for the rest of the job.

options.text: Submit the variation today and keep the gang digging while it's processed — stopping a trench gang costs money, the extent will be covered within a day or two, the inspector has already recorded the finding and the line was always going here.
options.feedback: Knowingly continuing outside your permitted extent after being formally told is deliberate unlawful occupation — fixed penalties, potential stop notice, and a client watching its own permit record being damaged.
options.criticalFailure: Continued street works beyond permitted extent after inspector's finding
options.consequence: The inspector returned to find the trench still advancing; the authority issued further fixed penalties and a direction to stop, and the client's permit performance was formally flagged.

options.text: Accept the finding without argument, pay the penalty when it arrives and put the variation in today, treating the occasional overrun as a known, budgeted cost of keeping a fast trench moving on this programme.
options.feedback: Accepting the sanction without fixing the planning process guarantees the next one — and authorities score utilities and contractors on these records when granting future permits.

eventPool.learningNote: The permitted extent, dates and hours are legal limits on your occupation of the highway. Track works progress against the permit daily, vary in advance rather than apologise afterwards, and treat the authority's inspectors as the client for the road — because for the highway, they are.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: During refuelling of the excavator in the working lane, the nozzle jams open and several litres of diesel spread across the road surface, running toward the gully five metres away.

options.text: Stop the transfer, dam the flow ahead of the gully with absorbents and seal it, absorb the rest, bag it as hazardous waste, report it per the environmental plan, then fix refuelling: drip trays, a second person, positions away from gullies.
options.feedback: Correct. The order is source, pathway, then clean-up: stop the flow, cut the route to the gully, absorb, dispose properly, report, and change the refuelling arrangement that made a jammed nozzle into a near-pollution.

options.text: Wash the diesel off the carriageway toward the gully with the water bowser before it spreads into the traffic lane and becomes a skid risk to motorcyclists in the queue.
options.feedback: You've just converted a contained spill into a pollution offence in a watercourse. Skid risk is managed with absorbent and signing, never by washing hydrocarbons into surface water drainage.
options.criticalFailure: Fuel spill washed into surface water gully
options.consequence: Diesel washed down the gully left a sheen at the brook outfall; the Environment Agency traced it to the works, served an enforcement notice and recovered clean-up costs from the contractor.

options.text: Spread sand from the reinstatement stockpile over it to soak it up, sweep it back onto the heap once it's dry, and finish the refuel — the gully is five metres away.
options.feedback: Sand slows it but the gully is still open, the contaminated sand still needs proper disposal, and diesel doesn't meaningfully evaporate — it migrates. And the refuelling set-up that caused this is unchanged.
options.consequence: Diesel ran under the sand into the gully and left a sheen at the outfall; a resident reported it, and the contaminated sand in the reinstatement stockpile had to be dug out and disposed of.

options.text: Stop the nozzle, contain the spill with the spill kit and seal the gully before it reaches the drain, then bag the used absorbents in with the general waste to keep the hazardous waste charge down — the volume is small and it's mostly absorbent.
options.feedback: Good containment, wrong ending — fuel-soaked absorbents are hazardous waste and misdescribing them into general waste is an offence that turns a well-handled spill into a paperwork prosecution.

eventPool.topic: Fuel spill response and refuelling controls
eventPool.learningNote: Spill response order: stop the source, block the pathway (dam ahead of the gully, seal the gully), absorb and contain, dispose of contaminated material as hazardous waste, report and record, then fix the arrangement — drip trays, supervised refuelling, and distance from drainage as the default.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: Ahead of the client's audit you discover the weekend's excavation inspection sheets were all completed this morning — backdated and signed by a supervisor who wasn't on site. He says he was 'just tidying the paperwork up'.

options.text: Quarantine the false sheets, record the truth that the weekend inspections were missed, inspect before anyone re-enters, investigate how the gap and the falsification happened, deal with the supervisor's conduct and report it up the line.
options.feedback: Correct. Statutory inspection records are legal documents. An honest gap is a management failure you can fix; a forged record is a criminal act that also destroys any defence the company had. The trench is unproven until genuinely inspected.

options.text: Withdraw the backdated sheets from the file, note the supervisor's conduct privately, and start a fresh register from today's inspection, so the audit sees only genuine records and nothing that was falsified.
options.feedback: Removing the evidence compounds the problem — the record should show what actually happened, including the missed inspections and how they were corrected. Concealment reads as cover-up to any investigator.
options.consequence: The client's auditor spotted the gap in the register and asked for the weekend sheets; finding them withdrawn, the audit escalated to a formal investigation and the supervisor was suspended.

options.text: Keep the tidied sheets in the file for the audit — the trench was dry and undisturbed all weekend, the boxes didn't move, and the inspections would almost certainly have passed.
options.feedback: Making false entries in statutory registers and using forged documents are criminal offences in their own right — unlimited fines and potential imprisonment, as prosecutions following fatalities have shown. 'Probably fine' is not an inspection.
options.criticalFailure: Retained falsified statutory inspection records
options.consequence: The client's auditor matched the sheets against gate records showing the supervisor was absent; the matter went to HSE, which opened an investigation into falsified statutory records.

options.text: Have the trench inspected today before anyone goes back in, keep the weekend sheets on file this once with a recorded verbal warning to the supervisor, and make it clear in front of the gang that backdating paperwork must never happen again.
options.feedback: The re-inspection is right — but accepting the false record leaves forged statutory documents in your system and tells the supervisor the practice is tolerated.

eventPool.topic: Statutory records — honesty, falsification and legal status
eventPool.learningNote: Inspection registers, permits and RAMS sign-offs are legal documents. Falsifying, forging or making false entries in them is a criminal offence separate from any underlying safety breach — people have gone to prison for altering records after incidents. If a control was missed, record that it was missed, fix it, and fix the system.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: A groundworker who spent last week in the flooded trench and around the drainage chamber calls in with a heavy 'flu' — fever, headache, muscle pain. His mate mentions rats around the spoil heap and that the man had a cut hand taped up with insulation tape.

options.text: Tell him to see a doctor today and mention possible rat contamination at work (leptospirosis risk), record it as possible work-related illness, then review controls: waterproof dressings, gloves, washing before eating, rat baiting — and brief the gang.
options.feedback: Correct. Leptospirosis (Weil's disease) starts like flu and can be fatal if untreated — early treatment depends on the doctor knowing about the occupational exposure. Occupational ill-health needs the same investigate-and-control response as an injury.

options.text: Tell him to rest at home and phone in when he's better — winter flu is going round the gang, he can self-certify for a week, and coming in ill would only spread it.
options.feedback: Flu-like symptoms after contact with rat-contaminated water and ground, with broken skin, is the classic leptospirosis presentation. Untreated it can cause organ failure. The occupational link is exactly what a GP needs to hear to test for it.
options.criticalFailure: Dismissed possible occupational disease as ordinary illness
options.consequence: Untreated, he was admitted to hospital with leptospirosis; the diagnosis was reported under RIDDOR and HSE asked why his symptoms and the rat exposure had not been acted on.

options.text: Send the whole gang for blood tests and stop all trench and chamber work until the results come back, so nobody else is exposed while the cause is confirmed.
options.feedback: Caution is better than dismissal, but a blanket shutdown isn't proportionate — the urgent actions are the sick worker's medical disclosure and fixing the exposure controls for everyone else.

options.text: Issue a site-wide safety alert that gloves must be worn in the trench and at the chamber, and have the supervisor check glove use on his rounds this week.
options.feedback: An alert doesn't help the man who is already ill, doesn't address the rat infestation or hygiene facilities, and gloves alone don't cover the cut-skin and hand-to-mouth routes.
options.consequence: The rat problem around the spoil heap continued and a second operative with an uncovered cut fell ill with flu-like symptoms; the client's audit raised a hygiene non-conformance.

eventPool.topic: Occupational health — leptospirosis and contaminated ground
eventPool.learningNote: Ill health kills far more construction workers than accidents do, and much of it starts invisibly. For wet ground, drainage and watercourse work: control rodents, cover cuts with waterproof dressings, provide washing before eating and drinking, and make sure workers tell their doctor what they do — early diagnosis of diseases like leptospirosis depends on it. Treat suspected occupational disease like any incident: record, investigate, improve controls.

modelAnswerNotes: No occupation of the highway until street works permits are confirmed; off-highway mobilisation used to protect the programme, and works tracked daily against permitted extent, dates and hours.
CDM duty holders appointed in writing by the utility client; F10 notified; street works law and CDM run in parallel — neither replaces the other.
Competence matched to risk: streetworks-qualified operatives and supervisors, trained TM crew, plant tickets, and confined space entry and rescue training verified before those activities.

Site set-up: compound and everything static in the car park corner; barriered pedestrian diversion on the footway; trench and plant inside the guarded working lane; safety zone never occupied; fuel and silt kept away from the gully; dedicated protection at the school crossing.
TM treated like temporary works: agreed layout, trained installers, safe set-out/removal sequence, and recorded drive-through/walk-through checks with a planned fallback for signals failure.

Permit to dig with located services on every break of ground; trial holes and positive identification before any mechanical digging near gas or the HV crossing; everything treated as live until proven otherwise.

TW register live and moving with the works: trench boxes verified against tabulated data per set-up (standard solution, checked); chamber shaft, gas main support and thrust blocks bespoke with independent checks; hold points at trench entry and permit to load for road plates.
Permits: dig, confined space, lane occupation, load, electrical isolation/HV proximity, and fusion/hot works — no more, no fewer.
Excavations inspected at every shift start and after rain, flooding or strikes; chamber entry only under a permit with tested atmosphere, top man and rehearsed retrieval-based rescue.
Lifting under LOLER: planned lifts, certified accessories, tag lines from outside the trench, nobody in the trench during pipe lowering or box moves, daily recorded quick hitch checks.

Environment: dewatering through settlement to a consented discharge, gully protection, contaminated spoil tested and segregated with duty-of-care records, spill response drilled, proactive resident and school communication.

Handover: permanent reinstatement to highway standards with compaction records, completion registered so the guarantee runs, and as-laid depths, materials and residual risks delivered into the health and safety file.
